name: Kira Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a data protection lawyer at Marlow Price, a firm of about a hundred and twenty lawyers, and most of my clients are charities, hospitals and housing associations. A normal day is a breach call in the morning, where someone has emailed a spreadsheet of patient names to the wrong person, then hours of redrafting privacy notices and data-sharing agreements. I like the hospital work, because it feels like the rules actually protect someone. What wears me out is the billing, six-minute units, every single day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said six-minute units. How does the rest of your week fit around that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My target is about 1,600 billable hours a year, and I'm usually a bit under, which is normal for my year group. I live with my partner Omar, who teaches chemistry at a secondary school, and we've got about eleven months of my salary saved for a flat deposit. I use the firm's AI drafting tool now and then for a first pass at a privacy notice, but I check every line, because I've seen it invent a regulation that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's close to what I see now, honestly. The tools are handy for a first draft and useless the moment a case gets messy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. I'd tell the team at Marlow Price that the hype was a sales pitch and the real job, judging what's fair with people's data, was always going to need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plan holds. I keep doing the hospital work, I make senior associate in two or three years, and Omar and I buy a flat. The only thing that changes is I'd stop feeling guilty for not using the tool more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep billing the same, keep my target and keep saving about £900 a month toward the deposit. I'd maybe sign up for the firm's short course on the new data rules for AI, because clients will still ask about them even if AI flops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit flat too, because part of me wanted something to shake up the six-minute grind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bit flat. What would you want shaken up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Billing in six-minute units is the most robotic thing about my job, and no robot ever made us do it. I'd want fewer hours logged and more time on the cases that matter, like the hospital ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, who at work would you still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paralegals, honestly. Even a small tool takes away the routine checking they do, and two of them are saving for law school. Routine screen work is exactly what even a weak AI eats first.

say: AI was mostly a **sales pitch**, and judging what's fair with people's data still needs a person.
I'd tell the team the **hospital work** never depended on the tool anyway.
think: My **career plan** holds: senior associate in two or three years.
Omar and I still buy a **flat** on the timeline we set.
The **paralegals** lose some routine checking even in this quiet version.
do: Keep my **billing target** of about 1,600 hours and keep the hospital clients.
Save about **£900 a month** toward the flat deposit with Omar.
Take the firm's short **course on AI rules**, since clients will still ask.
feel: A little **flat**, because the six-minute grind stays exactly the same.
S0.quote: Billing in six-minute units is the most robotic thing about my job, and no robot ever made us do it.
fieldNote: She's **secure** here: high pay, plenty of firms nearby and eleven months saved.
Her worry shifts straight to the **paralegals**, which fits her progressive outlook.
She admits she wanted **some change**, which she didn't expect to say.

steps.text: Keep the hospital clients and hit the 1,600-hour billing target
Save £900 a month toward a flat deposit with Omar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that one I can picture in our office by next spring. Half of what juniors do is writing and checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules on how firms use AI on client data, and I'd mean it. Online I'd probably share something about the people losing jobs first, the paralegals and the trainees, not the partners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm fine for a few years but the ladder under me disappears. If the firm stops hiring trainees, then in five years there's nobody to train and the partners stop needing mid-level people like me to supervise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the drafting tool properly instead of now and then, maybe an hour a day, once I'd seen colleagues trust it. I'd also apply for the firm's AI governance group, because clients will pay for advice on exactly this. And I'd push our savings up to about £1,200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for this year, but I'd notice every empty desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd notice the empty desks. Whose desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paralegal friend Priya has spent three years checking contracts line by line, and Steady Disruption is a world where that job just quietly isn't there. Priya is the one I'd buy lunch for and not know what to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any of this change your plans with Omar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still buy the flat, but a smaller one, maybe one bedroom instead of two. Omar's job feels safer than mine, which is a strange thing to say about a teacher's pay.

say: Firms need **clear rules** on using AI with client data.
The **paralegals and trainees** go first, not the partners who decide.
think: I'm fine for a few years, but the **career ladder** under me disappears.
Fewer trainees now means fewer **mid-level** people needed later.
do: Use the **drafting tool** about an hour a day once colleagues trust it.
Apply to the firm's **AI governance group** this year.
Raise savings to about **£1,200 a month**.
feel: **Uneasy**, though not afraid for this year.
Every **empty desk** in the office would stay on my mind.
S1.quote: My paralegal friend Priya has spent three years checking contracts line by line, and Steady Disruption is a world where that job just quietly isn't there.
fieldNote: She moves **once proven**: tool use goes up only after colleagues trust it.
She sees opportunity in **AI governance** advice, which is close to her own field.
The smaller flat shows she's quietly **hedging** while sounding steady.

steps.text: Use the firm's drafting tool an hour a day for first drafts
Join the firm's AI governance group and study the new AI rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even make senior associate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be loud about it. I'd say the companies making these systems should pay for the transition, and I'd back a tax on AI profits to fund retraining and wage support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2029. Almost everything I do is thinking work at a screen, so the robots coming three years later make no difference to me. Clients would ask the AI for the privacy notice and pay a partner to sign it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next six months I'd cut spending hard and hold the flat money as cash, not a deposit. I'd apply to the national data protection regulator, because public bodies change slower and someone has to check the machines. I'd also join the campaign for an AI profits tax, properly, not just online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots make no difference to you. Is there any hands-on side to your work at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the only hands-on thing I do is shaking a client's hand at the end of a meeting, and nobody bills for a handshake. Maybe sitting with a scared hospital manager after a breach, but that's comfort, not law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Omar that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Omar we're putting the flat on hold and living on his salary for a while, which would hurt my pride. Then I'd say we're lucky, because a teacher in a classroom gets a few more years than a lawyer at a desk.

say: The **AI companies** should pay for the transition through a profits tax.
Retraining and **wage support** must be funded before the jobs vanish.
think: My job is likely **gone by 2029**, since nearly all of it is screen work.
The **robots' later date** gives me nothing; my work is all thinking.
do: Hold the **flat deposit** as cash and cut spending in the first six months.
Apply to the **data protection regulator**, where change comes slower.
Join the campaign for an **AI profits tax** in person.
feel: Some **hurt pride** at living on Omar's salary.
S2.quote: Honestly, the only hands-on thing I do is shaking a client's hand at the end of a meeting, and nobody bills for a handshake.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** within a year of AGI, so the mood is alarmed.
She sees clearly that **robots' later date** doesn't help a desk lawyer.
Her household hedge is **Omar's teaching**, which she thinks lasts longer.

steps.text: Pause the flat purchase and keep the deposit as cash
Cut eating out and the summer holiday in the first six months
Apply for a job at the national data protection regulator
Campaign in person for a tax on AI company profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is different. I'd be thirty-two, which feels like enough time to turn around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as before about making the AI firms pay, but I'd add that five years is enough to plan if governments start now. I'd be pushing for that at the firm's diversity and wellbeing group, odd as that sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my firm job lasts maybe three or four years and then thins out. Five years lets me move to the regulator side on purpose instead of in a panic, and that matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time master's in technology law next autumn, paid from savings, about £12,000. In year three or four I'd move to the regulator or a hospital trust's in-house team. Omar and I would still buy the flat, but only something we could pay on his salary alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind of anxious you can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a flat you could pay on Omar's salary alone. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-bedroom flat in my postcode on a teacher's salary is a fantasy, so a five-year warning means a one-bed further out on the tram line. I'd rather that than a big mortgage on a job I can see ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a trainee starting at Marlow Price in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new trainee at Marlow Price to learn the AI inside out and also learn to sit in a room with frightened people. The second skill is the one I'd bet on.

say: Five years is **enough to plan** if governments start now.
AI firms should still **pay for retraining**, but there's time to build it.
think: My **firm job** probably thins out after three or four years.
Five years lets me move to the **regulator side** on purpose, not in a panic.
do: Start a part-time **master's in technology law** next autumn, about £12,000.
Move to the **regulator** or a hospital trust's in-house team by year four.
Buy a flat we can afford on **Omar's salary** alone.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way she can act on.
S3.quote: A two-bedroom flat in my postcode on a teacher's salary is a fantasy, so a five-year warning means a one-bed further out on the tram line.
fieldNote: The **extra three years** turn panic into a plan, but her income could still shrink.
Her bet is on **human comfort** in hard moments, not on legal drafting.
She keeps the **flat** but sizes it to the safer household income.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in technology law, about £12,000
Move to the regulator or a hospital in-house team by year four
Buy a one-bed flat further out that Omar's salary covers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, probably with a kid by then, so the timing is almost worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want the profession, the law society and the government planning now for what happens to people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I get to senior associate and maybe near partner just as the ground goes. I'd be at the peak of my pay and the start of having kids exactly when the work disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the tech law master's, but slower, over three years. I'd use the AI tools properly from year two so I know what they can't do. And I'd join the young lawyers' network at the law society to push for a real transition plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow, background way. Like a bill you know is coming in the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the timing is almost worse. Why worse than five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years' warning I'd be standing at the top of the ladder at thirty-seven, with a baby, just when the ladder gets taken away. At thirty-two I'd still have been light enough to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might push us to have a child sooner, maybe at thirty-one, while my salary is still solid. Omar thinks that's a terrible reason to have a baby, and he's probably right.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and wasting it would be foolish.
The **law society** and government should plan the transition now.
think: I'd hit **peak pay** just as the work goes.
A **child** at that age makes the drop much harder.
do: Do the **tech law master's** slowly over three years.
Use the **AI tools** properly from year two to learn their limits.
Join the **young lawyers' network** to push for a transition plan.
feel: **Anxious** in a slow, background way, like a bill on its way.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning I'd be standing at the top of the ladder at thirty-seven, with a baby, just when the ladder gets taken away.
fieldNote: She sees **ten years** as hitting her at the worst life stage, not as safe.
Her plans shift toward **children sooner**, which Omar questions.
She keeps a **collective** answer alongside her personal one, true to her outlook.

steps.text: Do the tech law master's part-time over three years
Use the firm's AI tools daily from year two
Join the law society's young lawyers' network on AI transition
Talk with Omar about having a child around thirty-one

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no plan, and the hospital clients would just stop calling. What would help is a funded transition, paid by the AI companies, that covers rent while people like me retrain, and regulators hiring people who understand data.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how my partner's job changes the picture. Omar's work with teenagers is the safest thing in our house, and people with two desk jobs don't have that cushion. I'd rather be the person who checks the machine than the one it replaced.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the person who checks the machine than the one it replaced.
portrait: A 27-year-old **data protection lawyer** at a mid-size firm, serving charities, hospitals and housing associations.
She lives with Omar, a **chemistry teacher**, with eleven months saved toward a flat.
She uses AI **now and then** and moves further only once colleagues trust it.
Calm in AI Plateau, she grows **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 and plans a move to the regulator.
She blames **AI companies** for the cost and wants them to fund retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time to plan and her clients would stop calling.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded transition** paid by AI companies, covering rent during retraining.
**Regulators hiring** lawyers who understand data and can check the machines.
